I've done a lot of technical support work for software. Before I did that, I thought tech support people knew everything. After doing tech support jobs at a couple different companies, I now understand tech support people often don't have any more answers than the people calling for help; the difference is how they approach problems. Tech support people need to be able to ask the right questions to get the most complete idea of the scenario, and double-check often important details which most people never consider. Those jobs allowed me to related to my mechanic and to my doctor in new ways! The skills picked up from troubleshooting "my software doesn't work" easily translate to things like "my car doesn't work" and "my body doesn't work."

There's also a lot more critical thinking involved in tech support — and probably most jobs — than should be necessary. On top of doing the work we're paid to do (fix software, fix cars, fix illness) we also have to deal with nonsensical bureaucracy and idiotic corporate policies. That stuff alone could drive people to insanity!

At least "my software doesn't work" doesn't have the same importance as "this person is dying" — even if the customer doesn't see it that way! I would never get into nursing. That seems way to stressful for me.

What is the mechanical advantage of an average claw hammer?

[Mechanical Advantage] = [Distance Handle to Fulcrum] / [Distance Fulcrum to nail]

Handle to fulcrum is about 30cm or 12"

Fulcrum to nail is about 25mm or 1"

So we have 12 / 1 = ~12

Hi dogmatic, welcome to devhelp and thank you for subscribing :)

I've always wondered what COBOL is like. I lean more towards web dev (i.e. php, .net, etc.) than software dev, but have been experimenting in the past with c, c++, c#, java, etc.

I'm really curious, how often do you get to use COBOL and is it in great demand now a days? It seems to have picked up quite a bit of popularity over the recent few years.

In my (atypical) case, the php is replaced with COBOL. The html is 'marked' where substitutions are to be made. The http server routes requests to COBOL. Cobol accesses db, flat files, business rules. Results prepared and substituted in html which is then sent back to http server. Same exact role as php.

In answer to your question of frequency: I code cobol every day, as a web dev would code php every day. The language is popular with big organizations. Orgs that own and operate mainframe computers (govt, banks, ins companies).

The reason cobol is in demand (the main reason) is that there is usually a 40-50 year old codebase which is not easily )nor cheaply) moved to 'the cloud' etc... Also many 3rd world developers have Master's degrees in compsci and are trained in cobol and are willing to work for less than prevailing wage for software dev.

"Hey baby, you still awake?" read the midnight text. "Been thinking a lot about you ;)"

It had been only a week since the messy break up, but I thought it would take longer for the sloppy text messages to come rolling in. But it was Saturday night, and clearly the booze was flowing on the other end, so roll in they did.

In a moment, the screen was filled with pictures of myself I'd posted to Facebook the last week. She'd been giving me the silent treatment, but here was all the evidence that she was watching my every move along the way.

"Who's that handsome boy? ;)"

I don't know if she meant to show me she cared or was trying to hit on me but it was coming off as downright disturbing in the way that makes your spine tingle a little.

I stared at the texts in a tired stupor for a moment and then decided that any response was worth far more effort than the situation justified. My head hit the pillow and I was out like a lightbulb.

The next morning I woke up to a note on the vacant pillow next to me.

"Maybe next time you'll reply"

If a text was enough to make my spine tingle the note was almost enough to make me piss myself. I froze in bed staring at it, and then slowly got up. How did she get in? Is she still in here?

In my living room I found my leather couch torn to shreds. The stuffing was strewn around the room, and where there wasn't stuffing there was broken glass from a variety of objects - picture frames, glasses and bottles I left out and some vases I bought at an auction.

If there's one thing that she went after with a vengance, it was my bookself. I could see pages ripped from fitness manuals and shreds of all of my favorite books by late forward-thinking authors. I spied a page of Catch-22 stuffed into one of the deep gashes in my couch. At least there was some beautiful irony in all of this.

The weirdest thing about all of it though was another note, affixed to what was left of my coffee table by way of my kitchen knife.

It read "THIS IS A SAFE SPACE."
